taxes.base: Taxable income of individuals: wages, business income, investment income and net capital gains, after deductions.
taxes.payer: Individuals; employers withhold it from wages (PAYG withholding).

rate.headline: Residents 0%–45% (15% to 45% above A$18,200)
details: Resident rates for 2026–27: nil to A$18,200; 15% from A$18,201 to A$45,000; 30% to A$135,000; 37% to A$190,000; 45% above. The lowest rate was 16% until 30 June 2026 and falls to 14% from 1 July 2027.
Non-residents pay 30% from the first dollar up to A$135,000 and the same higher rates above.
The 2% Medicare levy is charged on top, and shown as a separate core.

instruments.explanation: The biggest source of Australian revenue, collected by the Commonwealth alone. States left the income tax field in 1942, and there is no state or local income tax.
exceptions: Capital gains are taxed as income, with a 50% discount for assets held over 12 months by individuals.

taxes.base: Taxable income of residents (the same base as income tax).
taxes.payer: Resident individuals; low-income earners are reduced or exempt.

rate.headline: 2% of taxable income
details: A surcharge of 1% to 1.5% applies to higher earners without private hospital cover (the Medicare levy surcharge).

instruments.explanation: A flat levy on top of income tax that helps pay for the public health scheme; legally it goes into general revenue, not a special fund.
exceptions: Reductions and exemptions for low incomes, some foreign residents and certain medical conditions.

taxes.base: The taxable value of non-cash benefits that employers give employees (cars, loans, entertainment, housing).

rate.headline: 47% of the grossed-up taxable value
details: The FBT year runs from 1 April to 31 March; the rate is 47% from 31 March 2023 to 31 March 2027.

instruments.explanation: The employer, not the employee, pays tax on benefits, at the top personal rate including the Medicare levy.
exceptions: Several exempt benefits (for example work-related items and eligible electric cars) and reductions for charities and hospitals.

taxes.base: Taxable income of companies, with imputation credits for dividends paid to resident shareholders.

rate.headline: 30%; 25% for small base-rate entities
details: 30% for most companies; 25% for base rate entities, which have aggregated turnover under A$50 million and no more than 80% passive income.

instruments.explanation: The Commonwealth’s second-largest tax. Dividends carry franking credits so that company tax paid is credited to shareholders.

names.official: Income tax paid by superannuation funds

taxes.base: Contributions received and investment earnings of superannuation funds.
taxes.payer: The funds, out of members’ savings.

rate.headline: 15% on contributions and earnings
details: Concessional contributions and earnings in the accumulation phase are taxed at 15% inside the fund; earnings backing retirement-phase pensions are tax-free up to the transfer balance cap.

instruments.explanation: Employers must pay a percentage of wages (the superannuation guarantee, 12% from 1 July 2025) into private funds; the Commonwealth taxes the funds, not the payments themselves.

names.official: Withholding taxes on non-residents (dividends and interest)

taxes.base: Unfranked dividends and interest paid to non-residents.
taxes.payer: Non-resident recipients; the payer withholds it.

rate.headline: 30% dividends; 10% interest
details: 30% on unfranked dividends and 10% on interest, usually reduced by tax treaties.

instruments.explanation: A final tax on investment income going abroad.

taxes.base: Most supplies of goods and services consumed in Australia, and imports.
taxes.payer: Consumers; businesses charge it and claim credits for the GST they pay.

rate.headline: 10% of the price
details: A single rate of 10% (s. 9-70). GST-free supplies include basic food, most health and education services, and exports; financial supplies and residential rent are input-taxed.

instruments.explanation: The Commonwealth collects the GST but pays all of it to the states and territories as untied grants, distributed by a horizontal equalisation formula.

names.official: Excise duties and levies (fuel, tobacco, alcohol and others)

taxes.base: Fuel and petroleum products, tobacco and alcohol made in Australia, plus small levies on agricultural production and statutory corporations.
taxes.payer: Producers and manufacturers; passed on in prices. Imports pay equivalent customs duties.

rate.headline: Per litre or per stick, indexed twice a year
details: Fuel and alcohol rates are indexed to CPI each February and August; tobacco rates to average weekly earnings each March and September.
Tobacco in 2026: about A$1.55 per cigarette (sticks up to 0.8 g, from 1 September 2026).
A temporary cut in the fuel excise applied from 1 April 2026; the full rate was restored from 3 August 2026.

instruments.explanation: A group that the ABS reports together: the largest part is the excise on fuel and tobacco, and spirits and beer bring in the rest. Only the Commonwealth may levy excise (s. 90 of the Constitution).
exceptions: Fuel tax credits refund the excise on fuel used in business off public roads.

taxes.base: The customs value of imported goods, by tariff classification and origin.

rate.headline: Free or 5% on most goods
details: Rates are set per item in the Customs Tariff; goods from free-trade-agreement partners are often free. Excise-equivalent duties apply to imported fuel, alcohol and tobacco.

instruments.explanation: Collected by the Australian Border Force at the border. Duty is among the smaller sources because most tariffs are low or zero.

names.official: Other Commonwealth taxes (sales taxes, payroll and labour force, use of goods and activities)

taxes.base: A set of smaller taxes and levies that the ABS groups together, such as the luxury car tax, the wine equalisation tax and the passenger movement charge.

rate.headline: Different rate for each tax
details: Grouped from three ABS lines: general (sales) taxes 2,223, taxes on employers’ payroll and labour force 1,725 and taxes on the use of goods and performance of activities 12,343, plus 135 of minor items.

instruments.explanation: The remainder of Commonwealth taxation after the named taxes. The ABS does not break this down further in the table used.

taxes.base: Wages paid by employers above a tax-free threshold (grouped employers are added together).

rate.headline: Set by each jurisdiction, roughly 5%–7%
details: New South Wales charges 5.45% of wages above A$1.2 million in 2026-27; other states and territories use their own thresholds and rates.

instruments.explanation: The biggest state tax. Each jurisdiction runs its own system under a common model, with extra rules for wages paid across state lines.
exceptions: Charities and some public bodies are exempt; apprentices and trainees have concessions in most jurisdictions.

taxes.base: The price of land and buildings (and some business assets) when they change hands.

rate.headline: Sliding scale up to about 5.5%–7%
details: New South Wales in 2026-27: from A$1.25 per A$100 on low values to A$5.50 per A$100 above A$1.29 million, and A$7.00 per A$100 on premium residential land above A$3.87 million.

instruments.explanation: A large and volatile state tax that moves with the property market. Several states have been replacing it with land tax for first-home buyers.
exceptions: First-home buyer concessions and exemptions vary by state.

taxes.base: The unimproved value of land held above a threshold.
taxes.payer: Landowners; the main home is exempt.

rate.headline: Set by each jurisdiction on land value above a threshold
details: New South Wales applies a tax-free threshold of about A$1.08 million and a premium rate band for land above about A$6.6 million.

instruments.explanation: A tax on investment property, vacant land and commercial land. The principal place of residence is not taxed.
exceptions: Primary production land and the main home are exempt.

names.official: Motor vehicle taxes (registration, transfer duty on vehicles)

taxes.base: Owning and registering vehicles, and transfers of vehicle ownership.

rate.headline: Set by each jurisdiction
details: Registration charges depend on the vehicle and use; stamp duty on registration or transfer is charged on the value.

instruments.explanation: Registration fees and stamp duty on vehicles, as recorded by the ABS in the taxation statistics.

taxes.base: Gaming machines, casinos, lotteries and race and sports betting.

rate.headline: Set by each jurisdiction on revenue or turnover
details: Gaming-machine taxes are the largest component.

instruments.explanation: States license and tax gambling. Gaming machine taxes bring in about 60% of the total.

names.official: Taxes on insurance (stamp duty on insurance, contributions to fire brigades)

taxes.base: Insurance premiums (general, vehicle third-party, life) and insurers’ contributions to fire services.

rate.headline: Set by each jurisdiction on premiums

instruments.explanation: State duty on insurance premiums and the contributions that insurers pay to fund fire brigades.

taxes.base: Other property taxes, government borrowing guarantee levies, franchise taxes, excises and levies, and other taxes on the use of goods and performance of activities.

instruments.explanation: The remainder of state taxation after the named taxes, grouped from the ABS table.

taxes.base: The value of land (and in some states improvements) within the council area.
taxes.payer: Landowners; landlords may pass them on to tenants.

rate.headline: Set by each council within state limits
details: Councils set a rate in the dollar (and often a minimum charge); several states limit annual increases, for example the NSW rate peg and Victoria’s rate cap.

instruments.explanation: The one significant tax of local governments, levied on the land value of every property.
exceptions: Crown land, schools, churches and charities are often exempt or rebated.
